articles.title: Trump official feels heat as he calls in massive air force to fight small fire near home
articles.description: When an unattended campfire near Idaho's Sawtooth National Forest grew into what would become the seven-acre Cabin Creek Fire on July 12, the Forest Service didn't send a truck and a crew. It sent an air armada – helicopters, air tankers, tactical planes and a Black Hawk. Nine aircraft in all, converging on a blaze so small and so easily reached by ground crews that veteran officials say the response defies explanation, except for one detail, reported the Washington Post . The fire started 15 miles from the mega-ranch of Michael Boren, the Donald Trump-appointed undersecretary who oversees the federal agency he called for help. According to two Forest Service officials, Boren phoned regional and national offices repeatedly that day, including once in the middle of the night, demanding to know why more aircraft weren't already in the air and when reinforcements would arrive to battle the blaze. The Washington Post's flight-path analysis found aircraft streamed in from across the West, including a tanker pulled off another Nevada fire, for an operation that lasted a few hours and burned through roughly $114,000 in federal money. Compare that to how the same agency handled a nearly identical fire weeks earlier, when a 21-acre blaze near Sugarloaf, Idaho, on June 25 drew just three aircraft for about 13 minutes. Cabin Creek, at less than half that size, got triple the aircraft for a mission stretching hours. "I can't think of a time in my 38-year career where I saw a response like that for a five-acre fire," said Steve Ellis, a 38-year Forest Service veteran and former BLM deputy director. "It sounds like it was overkill." One official with direct knowledge of the calls went further, describing Boren's conduct as "putting pressure on staff to throw more resources at" the fire. At least some aircraft were pulled from fires burning elsewhere in Idaho, a state juggling three separate wildfires that same day under a historic heat dome. The nation's fire preparedness level stood at four out of five when Cabin Creek broke out, and three days later it hit the maximum level 5 – the earliest that's happened in a decade. Former fire officials warned that funneling scarce aircraft toward one undersecretary's backyard, while the rest of the West burned, is exactly the kind of favoritism the national coordination system is designed to prevent. A spokesman for the Agriculture Department denied Boren was simply conducting routine oversight when he repeatedly called for assistance with the fire near his property. “Boren is expected to have regular contact with the agencies he oversees," said department spokesman Michael Abboud. "The fact that a senior government official would be monitoring and communicating with other government officials about an event he oversees is a non-story ... At no point did he pressure leadership or order more resources to fight this or any other fire.”

articles.description: Twenty-one birds released on Bodmin Moor where it is hoped they will one day return to produce their own young They took a little coaxing at first – after all, they had got used to a safe, comfortable aviary tucked away in woodland on the edge of Bodmin Moor. But after a few minutes, the birds stepped out into freedom and the bolder ones were soon soaring into the blue, the first white storks to be released into the wilds of Cornwall. Yan Swiderski, the founder of the Cornwall Stork Project , had tears in his eyes. “I do feel a bit emotional,” he said. He sounded a little like a proud father wanting to play down the achievements of his offspring – and failing. “They’re a little bit clumsy at the moment. articles.title: Homeowners continue cleanup after EF-1 tornado ravages neighborhoods in Northwest Indiana
articles.description:
Laura Ramos said she grabbed her cat and hunkered down in her bathtub Tuesday after her phone sounded an alarm warning that a tornado was headed her way.

Moments later, a tornado with wind gusts of 86 to 110 mph tore through her Munster, Indiana, neighborhood, knocking down power lines, uprooting trees and buckling sidewalks. The National Weather Service confirmed the EF-1 tornado touched down on the north side of town.

“It’s true what they say that it sounds like a train going over your roof,” said Ramos, 59.

Indiana Gov. Mike Braun declared a state of emergency Thursday in response to widespread damage in Northwest Indiana from this week’s severe storms that brought flooding and tornadoes to the state. Weather officials also confirmed an EF-2 tornado touched down in St. John, Indiana.

“Hoosiers’ safety is my top priority,” Braun said in a statement. “Our state response is fully mobilized, resources are moving where they’re needed, and we will continue working around the clock to support every impacted community.”

Braun also deployed the Indiana National Guard to help communities in Lake County clear tree debris, according to the Lake County Homeland Security and Emergency Management Agency.

Ramos' home was damaged when the tornado knocked down two of her trees, causing one to land on her house. On Thursday morning, her sister-in-law and brother-in-law drove in from Chicago to help her with the cleanup.

After the tornado passed, Ramos said she was overcome with emotion as she surveyed the damage to her neighborhood. She moved into her home in the 8400 block of Moraine Avenue in 2009 and said she barely recognized the area after the storm.

“I made the mistake of going on a walk around the block, and I broke down and cried because everybody’s front yards were flipped over,” she said.

Though she suffered damage to her roof, Ramos said it could have been much worse.

On Thursday afternoon, several of Ramos’ neighbors were seen sawing through fallen trees and raking up leaves and debris. The steady hum of generators could also be heard as residents worked to keep their homes powered.

Ramos said she only had a small generator with enough power to charge her cellphone.

Thousands remained without power Thursday after the severe storms knocked out service for a majority of customers.

NIPSCO said late Thursday morning it had restored service for 75,000 of the 313,000 electric customers who lost service. The utility service said it was the largest outage event in its history.

It was unclear how long it would take to restore power. Many residents in Munster and Hammond said they were prepared to remain without electricity through at least the weekend, while some expected the outages to last even longer.

At a Hammond gas station, cars lined up Thursday to fill gas cans to fuel generators keeping homes powered after the storm.

Gil Mellendorf, of Munster, stopped at the BP at 6906 Hohman Ave. to get gas for the generators at his home. The gas station was also running on generators.

Mellendorf said his street flooded during Tuesday’s storm, and his biggest concern was keeping the sump pump running to prevent his home from flooding.

“It’s a lot going on right now,” said Mellendorf, 67. “But we’re veterans when it comes to storms.”

Mellendorf said he had already spent more than $100 since Tuesday to keep his generator running, adding that a tank of fuel typically lasts about 10 hours.

Munster officials said power was restored in some parts of town, but crews were working long hours to fix remaining outages, and urged residents to make way for utility and emergency crews.

“We know this is a stressful time, and we're grateful for your patience and cooperation,” town officials said in a statement. “A little space goes a long way in helping our crews get Munster back up and running safely.”
